title: The Woman Who Stayed
passages:
At eleven-oh-eight the ebb leaned hard against the Marrow's stern, and Rusk's dead barge had to swing clear or take the turn broadside and stove itself on the customs-house columns. Bayo took the wheel. Sol stayed at his shoulder with her hands on the spoke-box, watching him like she expected him to bolt.

Salas stood aft by the winch drum, one hand on the brake, his coat dripping salt water. He had risen off the drum when the bell rang, and he watched Bayo with full awareness of their history, confirming Bayo's face showed no change.

"True line," Bayo said. He killed the auxiliary and let the current yaw them. "Off the columns, not his poles. Rusk's markers are forty meters wrong, and he knows it."

"Then why's he still holding the mouth?" Sol said.

"Because he's patient," Bayo said. "And because he's got nothing else to do but wait for us to come up heavy." He eased the throttle. The Marrow's screws bit water, and the boat slid forward, close enough that Sol could see the rust scored into the ferry ribs jutting from the channel wall. Rusk's barge groaned, its cables singing as it pivoted on the lanyard, swinging its broad stern away from the gap just before the ebb could catch it and pin it against the drowned span.

Rusk's voice carried from the water, thin but clear: "Settle back, then. I'll sit right here."

Bayo didn't answer. He held the wheel steady while the Marrow threaded the gap, the columns sliding past on either side close enough to touch the ferry ribs. Sol kept her breath even, not touching the wheel.

"Through," Bayo said.

Sol let out the breath she'd been holding. "Rusk said he'd wait."

"He will," Bayo said. "Right up until he decides he won't."

The barge settled back across the channel mouth behind them, Rusk still in the water at its port side, lanyard taken up on his arm, holding the Stair shut while his arm rested. He called after them, voice rising over the water: "I'll be here when you come up heavy."

Sol turned to the compass box and set course for Mercy General's drowned flank. The bell had rung two notes. Mara was waiting, or whatever was left of her. And the season bell would seal the channel before they could run back out.

"Full ahead," Sol said.

Bayo's hands stayed on the wheel. "Aye, Captain."

Sol didn't look at him. She had heard him make that promise before.

They made the hospital at eleven-twenty. Sol laid the Marrow's port flank along the drowned tower's loading dock, where a mooring bollard still stood proud of the water, and Wren went over the side with the bow line and made it fast to the bollard with two turns and a hitch she could do in the dark. The Marrow stopped fighting the ebb and sat.

Nia was at the rail with her arms crossed, watching the black windows go up and up. Salas stood aft with his hand on the winch brake, not helping, not in the way either.

"Stairhead landing's at forty-one meters," Wren said, coming back aboard. "The high ward's at twenty-four. The Line sits at thirty-eight."

Dey was already in the last good bottle rig off the boat's rack, two stage bottles clipped at his chest, a full mask pushed up on his forehead. "So I lose three meters of myself and then I'm in the clear," he said. "Cheap seats."

"It doesn't come back when you get shallow," Sol said. "That's the whole trouble with the Line. It quits and it stays quit."

"I know what it does."

"Then you know what you're spending."

Wren went over his seals anyway, thumb around the mask skirt, hand on the bottle valve, because his own scrubber was on Teo's chest topside and until he had another one he didn't get to sign off on himself. She clipped the wire to his harness — a pencil-thin cable that trailed back to the Marrow's radio box, so topside could hear every word either of them said — and put her hand flat on his chest plate.

"You lead," Sol said. "You call the turn. You say the word, we all come up."

"I'll call it," Dey said, and went over the side.

The stairwell was a throat. Water at the bottom of it, black and still, the lamp beams going up through it and dying about four meters on. They swam the first flight and the second, Dey's fins kicking once, twice, unhurried. On the third landing a curtain rail had come down across the passage, and a length of cable with it, and Dey stopped to free it and strop it off the rail so the bag would ride up with them.

"Give me the—" he said. His hands were already doing it. "The knot. The loop that doesn't slip."

"Bowline," Wren said.

"Bowline," he said, and tied it, and it was a good one, because his hands had never been down here.

Above the fourth landing he turned and put two fingers on her shoulder plate and started a word and didn't finish it. He tried again. She watched his eyes behind the mask go looking around the inside of his own head for her.

"Wren," she said.

"Wren," he said, easy, like it had never left, and swam on.

At the fifth landing he stopped dead on the treads with the lamp pointed at nothing and said, through the wire, "What are we doing?"

"Going up to the ward," Wren said. "Twenty-four meters. Two flights."

"Right," he said. He went up. He didn't ask again, and he didn't say anything about having asked.

Wren kept the slate in her left hand where she could see it. The slate was her whole trade: a palm-sized recorder that logged a diver's depth, gas, and voice, everything a person said and everything they dropped. Hers had been running the whole climb. She scrolled it with her thumb while she finned, and there it was, two entries four seconds apart, his voice in both of them, same words, same flatness: *what are we doing.*

Free crew. He'd said it twice at the dock to anyone who'd stand still. She had spent a year learning which truths to file down to size, and she shut her mouth on the easy one.

"How far to the landing?" Dey said.

"Two flights," Wren said. "You just asked me."

"How far to the landing?" he said, and his lamp was already on the landing's edge, the last flight of treads, the ceiling of the water above them gone silver and thin and only a body-length up, and he was reaching for it with his free hand like a man who had never in his life been told.

The water broke and Wren's mask came out into air.

Not boat air. This was thick — three atmospheres of the tower's held breath — and it leaned on her eardrums and tasted of rust and bleach and, under that, tinned fruit gone over in a warm cupboard. Dey got his mask onto his forehead, took in a lungful, and coughed until she put a hand flat between his shoulder plates.

"Slow," she said. "It weighs the same as the water did. Breathe it slow and it stops shoving."

They were in a ward, and the sea was in half of it. The deck tipped away toward the seaward wall with a black sheet of water lying over it, lifting and settling as the ebb pulled at the tower's flank. Past that line the beds stood in rows, mattresses rotted to grey slabs, a chart still clipped to bed six's rail with nobody's signature on it in fourteen months.

Dey's lamp found the clean patch first. Deck plating with no rust on it, four bolt holes with the bolts backed out, and a hand-span of floor swept bare all the way round.

"The cradle," he said.

"Say that again."

"The cradle. Where the case sat." He looked at her. "You already asked me."

"I know," Wren said.

Under the windows the tins were stacked in courses like brickwork. Hundreds of them, rinsed, dented, some filled with rainwater, the top course fed by a drip line spliced off a pipe joint. Ration tins, formula tins, the little ones with pull rings.

"Somebody's been busy," Dey said.

"Somebody's been alone," Wren said.

Her lamp went up the wall and found the rig. A hand bell hung off an IV pole lashed to a bracket that used to carry a light panel, brass gone green in the throat. Beneath it sat a lamp cell — a battery the size of a bread loaf — its leads running to a charge controller screwed down over the deck, and from the controller a cable climbing through a hole knocked in the ceiling toward the solar skin, the light-panels still glued to the tower's roof above the waterline, still standing in daylight, still trickling. The cable came back down spliced. No crimps, no heat-shrink, no torch. Butt joints in surgical tape off a crash cart, wrapped over and over, some gone hard as bark, every one of them made in the dark by somebody with one hand free.

Beside the bell, a wind-up timer sat on a bedpan with a brass governor spinning on top of it. Tick. Tick. A cord ran from the timer's hammer to the striker on the hand bell.

Wren crouched, put her lamp on it, and did not touch it.

"It rings itself," she said.

Four seconds later, in exactly the same voice: "Somebody's been busy."

The slate in her left hand logged both, one under the other, and she thumbed past them.

The stairwell water pushed, and Salas came up into it with his mask shoved back, breathing the thick air like a man with fourteen months' practice at worse. He got one elbow onto the deck and stopped there, half in, looking at the swept rectangle where the cold-case had sat. His face did nothing at all. Wren logged that too, because logging was the only thing she had left to offer anybody.

Nia came last, on the third stage bottle off the rack, small and fast, up over the lip on her hands with her mask already off and her hair flat to her skull. She got three steps into the ward and quit.

The bell rope was moving. It ran off the wheel of the hand bell, across the deck, over the sill of the seaward window, and it was going hand over hand — a pull, a slack, a pull — while the ebb sucked down past the frame.

At the far window, past the last row of beds, a woman stood with her back to the room. Grey blanket over her shoulders. One hand on the bell rope.

She didn't turn around.

She turned around.

Not at a sound, because nobody had made one. The ebb let go of the rope for a second and her arm came in with the slack, and the turn came out of that same small correction, the way a person turns a page.

Grey blanket pinned at one shoulder with a surgical clip. Hair cut short, badly, with something that had an edge. Her cheeks were gone in far enough that Wren could see the hinge of her jaw working. She was breathing about four times a minute, slow and deep, the way a diver breathes the last of a bottle when he means to be breathing tomorrow.

Forty, maybe. Lips cracked white. Alive.

Her eyes went over the room in order — four figures, the water at the seaward line, the tins, the lamp cell, the water again. They came to Nia and stopped the way they had stopped on the tins. Courteous. Interested in nothing.

Then she turned back to the window and put her weight on the rope.

The crank was the shaft of a car alternator bolted through a bed frame, and where a handle should have been somebody had jammed a length of gas pipe onto the square. She turned it forty times. Wren counted, because counting was the job. The needle on the lamp cell came up off the floor by a hair. Then three pulls on the bell rope, spaced. Then two fingers under the drip joint feeding the top course of tins. Then the crank again.

"Mama," Nia said.

The woman kept turning. Her eyes came round without her shoulders and she looked at Nia the way she'd looked at the beds.

Nia had the handle out of her belt by then, unwrapped from a rag she'd carried since the Kettle, and held it up on her flat palm. Steel worn bright, and the bright part was small — four shallow troughs where a hand had closed on it a thousand times. She held it against the pipe on the crank shaft. It would have fit.

The woman looked at it, and at the girl holding it, and nothing arrived anywhere behind her eyes.

"Do you have a name?" she said.

"I'm Nia." Her voice came out level, which cost her. "Nia Vos. You picked it. You said it was short enough to shout across a ward."

"Thank you," the woman said, and went back to the crank.

Salas came up over the lip on his elbows, got his knees under him and stayed there, streaming, looking at her. Fourteen months he had spent his air on that name, hand over hand on the valve, and Wren watched him get it into his mouth and out.

"Mara."

"That's me." She didn't slow down. "I'm the one who stays."

"In the pocket," he said. "Forty-two meters, off the pharmacy. You had a lamp and you took my—"

"I don't know you." Not unkind. She was busy. "Are you the one who comes at slack?"

"I'm the one who came back."

"You sang to me," Salas said. "Down there. You sang."

"She never sang." Nia didn't look away from her mother. "Singing's air."

The woman turned the pipe on the square, forty more, and the needle came up, and she said to the window, "It has to keep going or it all goes dark and stays dark," and Wren wrote it down word for word on the slate in her left hand, because it was the first whole sentence anybody had heard out of her in fourteen months and it was not for any of them.

Dey was crouched at the seaward line with his lamp on the water, where the ebb had stopped pushing and started to lean the other way.

"Wren," he said. "Whose kid is that?"

Wren logged it. She thumbed past it. She did not answer.

She let Dey's question sit on the slate with the rest of the dropped things and went to the cable instead, because the cable would answer.

Wren had spent her whole trade inside salvage like this — splices a person makes in the dark with fingers too cold to feel. She traced the butt joints up from the charge controller, the box that meters what comes off a panel into a battery, counted the tape, found one repair gone over three times because the first two had failed wet. Somebody had climbed to the ceiling hole on a bad hip to keep a bread loaf of a cell drinking off the solar skin — the light-panels still glued to the tower's roof, and daylight only reaching them from one side, and only in the afternoon.

The needle sat a hair above dead.

"She's been running it dry," Wren said. "Hand over hand to make it last. The crank's not for light."

"Then what's the pipe turn?" Nia asked. She had her mother's handle in her fist, the bright-worn one, and she was not putting it down.

Wren put her lamp on the timer. The governor, the hammer, the cord, the striker lined up on the bell's brass throat. Input, delay, output. The timer turned the crank's slack into a pull. The pull rang the bell.

But a hand bell doesn't need a battery. You don't spend fourteen months wiring a bell to a timer to make noise in an empty ward.

"It keeps them," she said.

"Keeps what."

"Voices." Her mouth had gone dry in the thick air. "It's a Caller. She takes a voice in and it holds it, and at slack it gives one back. She's not waiting on rescue. She's waiting on slack." She looked at Mara — the forty turns, the slow diver's breathing, the jaw working on nothing. "But it doesn't hold for free. You feed it. You put a voice in, and it keeps the voice, and it eats the part of you that made it."

Nia's grip tightened on the handle.

"Every time that timer rings itself," Wren said, and now it was coming, the whole shape of it, "she's put in an hour of her own. To keep two children cold and breathing in that case till somebody came. Fourteen months of hours, a spoonful at a time, so the cell stays lit and the case stays cold and the bell keeps its voice—"

"She's not hollow from going too deep," Dey said.

He was still crouched at the waterline, but he'd turned around, and enough of him was left to be funny, which was its own kind of gone.

"She spent it," Wren said. "On purpose. On you two."

Dey's lamp drifted over the drowned beds. "I came down here to die rich. One big score, buy my paper back. Instead I'm watching a woman go broke on purpose for strangers." He tapped his chest plate, the two stage bottles. "Would give her mine. But." He gestured at the whole rig, the timer, the rope. "Rules."

"How many's she got left?" Nia said.

Nobody answered. The bell had no gauge. Mara wasn't going to say.

Then the ebb quit.

Wren felt it before she saw it — the water at the seaward line stopped leaning and lay flat and black and still, the whole tower dropping into the twice-a-day slack that lasts about as long as a held breath. Dey's beam steadied on nothing. The bell rope came down off the window, loose.

Mara's hand rode in with the slack and stopped.

And the Caller rang itself, once.

Not Mara's.

It came out of the bell in a man's voice, ragged, worn down at the edges to nothing, the voice of somebody who had spent fourteen months shouting through a valve: "Mara."

Wren had Salas's slate out of the dry pouch at her hip before she decided to reach for it. She thumbed the scrub back to the mark she'd left in it and the slate said the word too, same voice, same ragged cadence, and the play count in the corner of the screen went from four to three.

Two sources. One word. Same breath.

The slate was a machine. Machines don't guess. Which left the other one.

Salas was on his feet. He had heard his own voice come out of a brass bell bolted to an IV pole, and his hand went up into the air like he meant to take the word back off it.

"That's mine," he said.

"It's yours."

"Then who's saying it?"

"You are. Off the slate, in the pocket, hand over hand on the valve." She turned the screen so he could see the log run by, fourteen months of a man saying one word in the dark. "And it's in the bell. You said her name at that window nine minutes ago. It gave it back at slack."

"So it listens."

"It keeps what it's given. Nothing else."

Salas looked at the bell for a while. "I've said that name ten thousand times. It's the only thing down there that was mine." His jaw worked. "And I still couldn't tell you whose it is."

Three plays left, and the cell window had gone amber at the corner, which meant the log died when the cell did. Wren put the slate away before she could finish pricing what three plays was worth.

The crank had stopped. Mara's hand had come off the pipe with the slack, and she was standing at the window with the rope in her fist, and she turned toward the bell — not toward Salas, not toward the girl — the way a woman turns toward a machine that has done the thing she built it to do.

"It's slack," she said. "I have to give it one."

"You just did," Wren said.

"That was given to me." Perfectly reasonable, the way weather is reasonable. Her eyes went along the row of them and stopped on Nia's mouth. "It has to be a voice."

Wren put herself in the way, and Mara waited behind her with the patience of a person who has all day and no idea why.

At the waterline Dey opened his mouth. Whatever he'd been carrying since the fifth landing, he was the kind of man who'd hand it over to be liked, and Wren got a palm across his face before the first sound got out.

"Not that one," she said. "Not any of them. Not out of you."

He said something into her hand. She left it there. Behind her fingers his eyes were doing the slow search again, going around and around the inside of his own head, and she watched him find her and lose the word for her in the same second, and keep quiet, because there was nothing left in that room a person could say and still have afterward.

"Everything said in this ward goes in," she said, low, for the three of them who could hold a sentence. "Every word out loud. So nobody says anything they want back."

Salas looked at the bell, then at his own mouth, and shut it.

Wren checked her watch. Slack had eight minutes left in it, near enough.

Nia crossed the deck with her mother's crank handle still in her fist. She didn't offer it again. She took the hand that wasn't on the rope and held it, and Mara let her, and looked down at the two hands joined with mild interest, the way you look at a knot you don't need.

On the bedpan the timer's governor spun down, and the hammer lifted, and the Caller drew breath for the next voice.
